content: 1. It is essential to promote access to information about treatment options tailored to the specific needs and developmental level of children and young people. This includes fostering supported decision-making processes to ensure informed choices are made. 2. Arrangements should be made to provide support for children, young people, and their families or caregivers during periods of increased need or transitions, such as puberty or starting or changing schools. 3. Beginning-to-read interventions should be implemented to enhance communication and academic performance in children with intellectual developmental disorders. These interventions include components such as phonological awareness, letter-sound instruction, and decoding. 4. Evidence supports the delivery of beginning-to-read interventions in school settings by both specialists (e.g., special education teachers or researchers) and non-specialists (e.g., teacher assistants). These interventions vary in intensity but commonly employ instructional strategies grounded in social learning theories and behavioral technologies. 5. Research gaps exist, as studies have not included individuals with intellectual developmental disorders who are dual-language learners. Intervention sessions typically occur in school settings, and further research is needed to address these gaps. 6. Early communication interventions using direct instruction approaches should be considered to improve expressive phonological skills and reduce stuttering in children with developmental speech disorders. Evidence suggests these interventions yield significant results, although data on receptive phonological skills and vocabulary acquisition remain limited. 7. For children who stutter, direct instruction approaches involve speech-language therapists working with parents to deliver behavior modification programs with strong reinforcement components. Studies indicate that treatment gains are maintained over time, suggesting lasting effects. 8. Structured physical exercise should be considered to improve development, including social and communication skills, in children and adolescents with autism. Activities such as planned sports games, aerobic exercise, cycling, and yoga can be conducted individually or in groups. 9. The World Health Organization recommends that children and adolescents engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, incorporating aerobic activities and muscleand bone-strengthening exercises at least three times a week. 10. Structured physical exercise programs should be adapted to meet the needs of children and adolescents with autism, including the use of visual supports, structured approaches, and caregiver involvement. These programs should be implemented within inclusive and enabling environments. 11. Task-oriented instruction should be considered to improve motor skills and task performance in children with developmental coordination disorders. This approach involves practicing specific tasks or occupations, such as task-specific training, cognitive motor approaches, and ecological interventions. 12. Specialized instructional techniques should be employed to improve academic performance, including writing skills, reading comprehension, and mathematics, in children and adolescents with developmental learning disorders. These techniques may include structured materials, visual models, alternative texts, and peer-assisted learning strategies. 13. Cognitive interventions aimed at enhancing communication and social competencies should be considered for children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disabilities. These interventions often involve computerized and adaptive cognitive exercises tailored to the child’s cognitive profile. 14. Structured physical exercise programs should also be considered for children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to improve motor skills, attention, executive functioning, and reduce anxiety and problem behaviors. Activities may include sports games, aerobic exercise, and yoga. 15. Research gaps highlight the need for more evidence on interventions for older adolescents and young adults, as well as the long-term effects of structured physical exercise and task-oriented instruction. Further studies are required to explore digital and virtual reality-based exercise programs tailored to these populations. 16. All children and adolescents with developmental disorders should have full access to health and social care services, including mental health services. Information about treatment options should be made accessible, and supported decision-making should be promoted. 17. Reasonable adjustments and adaptations, such as visual supports and structured approaches, should be made to ensure interventions are developmentally appropriate and inclusive for all children and adolescents with developmental disorders.
